title: Anatomy of a test: structure, matchers, async
objectives: Write a test as arrange-act-assert with `describe`/`it`, and build fresh state in `beforeEach` so tests can't leak into each other
Choose `toBe`, `toEqual`, `toStrictEqual`, `toMatchObject` or `toBeCloseTo` — or the `node:assert/strict` equivalent — for a given value
Predict which async tests pass without checking anything in Vitest 4, and fix them with `await`, `.resolves`/`.rejects` or `expect.hasAssertions()`
Use `.only`, `.skip` and `.todo` deliberately, and explain why a leftover `.only` fails the CI run

sources.title: Playwright docs: Best Practices (lint your tests)

questions.prompt: `const cart = new Cart()` sits at the top of a test file and every test uses it. "starts empty" passes when run alone but fails when the whole file runs. Why?

options.text: An earlier test mutated the shared cart; build a fresh one in `beforeEach`
Tests in one file run in parallel, so they race on the cart
The test is flaky; retry it until it passes
The cart should be created in `beforeAll` so it's ready before the tests

questions.explanation: Tests in a file run in order by default, and one object shared between them carries each test's changes into the next. That makes results depend on order and filtering — a deterministic leak, not flake. `beforeEach` gives every test its own cart. `beforeAll` runs once, so it shares the cart exactly like the top-level `const`.

questions.prompt: `expect(getUser()).toBe({ id: 1, name: "Ada" })` fails with `expected { id: 1, name: 'Ada' } to be { id: 1, name: 'Ada' }`. Why?

options.text: `toBe` uses `Object.is`, which asks whether both sides are the *same object*; two objects with equal contents aren't
The keys are in a different order internally
`getUser()` returns a class instance, and `toBe` checks the class
It's a Vitest display bug; the values differ in a way the message hides

questions.explanation: `toBe` is identity for objects — it passes only if both sides are the very same reference. For "same contents", use `toEqual` (or `toStrictEqual`). Key order doesn't matter to any of these matchers, and checking the class is `toStrictEqual`'s extra rule, not `toBe`'s.

questions.prompt: `createUser()` returns `{ name: "Ada", role: "admin", createdAt: "…" }` and `createdAt` changes every run. Which assertion passes while ignoring it?

options.text: `expect(user).toMatchObject({ name: "Ada", role: "admin" })`
`expect(user).toEqual({ name: "Ada", role: "admin" })`
`expect(user).toStrictEqual({ name: "Ada", role: "admin" })`
`expect(user).toBe({ name: "Ada", role: "admin" })`

questions.explanation: `toMatchObject` checks only the keys you list. `toEqual` is a full structural comparison, so the extra `createdAt` key fails it — it only forgives keys whose value is `undefined`. `toStrictEqual` is stricter still, and `toBe` compares identity.

questions.prompt: You'll write the partial-refund test next sprint and want the gap to stay visible in every test report until then. Which line?

options.text: `it.todo("refunds a partial order")`
`it("refunds a partial order", () => {})`
`it.skip("refunds a partial order", () => {})`
`// TODO: test partial refunds`

questions.explanation: `.todo` exists for exactly this: the report counts it separately as a test still to write. An empty `it` is worse than nothing — it has no failing `expect`, so it passes and the gap shows up as green. `.skip` is for a test that exists but is switched off, so it reads as "disabled", not "missing". A comment never appears in any report.

questions.prompt: A test does `import assert from "node:assert"` and `assert.equal(count, "1")` where `count` is the number `1`. What happens?

options.text: It passes — the default import is legacy mode, where `equal` uses `==`; import `node:assert/strict` instead
It fails — `assert.equal` is always strict
It throws a TypeError because the types differ
It throws because legacy mode was removed in Node 22

questions.explanation: Node's default `node:assert` is legacy assertion mode: `equal` and `deepEqual` use `==`, so `1 == "1"` passes. In strict mode (`node:assert/strict`), `equal` is `Object.is` and `deepEqual` behaves like `deepStrictEqual`. Legacy mode still exists — Node marks it "Legacy", not removed.

questions.prompt: `load(id)` resolves to `"Ada"`. Under **Vitest 4**, which of these tests passes even though it expects the wrong value?

options.text: `it("x", async () => { [1, 2].forEach(async (id) => { expect(await load(id)).toBe("Bo"); }); })`
`it("x", async () => { await expect(load(1)).resolves.toBe("Bo"); })`
`it("x", async () => { expect(await load(1)).toBe("Bo"); })`
`it("x", () => { expect(load(1)).resolves.toBe("Bo"); })`

questions.explanation: `forEach` ignores the promises its async callbacks return, so the test's own promise doesn't wait for them and the test is reported as passed. The failing `expect`s throw inside promises nobody awaits: if they settle while the worker is still running, Vitest fails the *run* with unhandled rejections (not attached to any test); if not, nobody ever sees them. The awaited forms obviously fail. The dangling `.resolves` is the subtle one: Vitest 4 auto-awaits it at the end of the test, so it *fails* (with a warning about the missing `await`), and Vitest 5 fails it outright.

questions.prompt: A PR leaves an `it.only` in a file. Locally the run is green; in CI the run fails. Why?

options.text: Vitest's `allowOnly` defaults to `!process.env.CI`, so CI rejects `.only` with "Unexpected .only modifier"
CI counts every test that `.only` skipped as a failure
CI ignores `.only`, runs everything, and a different test fails
`.only` is a Node-only feature that Vitest doesn't support in CI

questions.explanation: Locally `.only` is a convenience; in CI it would silently skip the rest of the file, so Vitest 4 refuses it by default and fails the run naming the modifier. Skipped tests aren't failures, and CI doesn't ignore the modifier — it rejects it. (Node's runner has its own switch: it honours `only` under `--test-only`.)

questions.prompt: `expect(parse("{")).toThrow(SyntaxError)` — `parse` throws on bad input. What happens?

options.text: The test fails with the raw `SyntaxError`: `parse` threw while building the argument, before `expect` ran
It passes — `toThrow` catches the error
It passes without checking anything, because the error is swallowed
`toThrow` throws a TypeError because it received `undefined`

questions.explanation: Arguments are evaluated before the call, so `parse("{")` throws before `expect` or `toThrow` exist. Nothing catches it; the test fails with the parser's own error. Write `expect(() => parse("{")).toThrow(SyntaxError)` so the matcher calls the function inside its own `try`.

prompts.prompt: Give every test a fresh cart, and assert the empty total with the matcher for primitives.
prompts.explanation: `beforeEach` runs before every test in the `describe`, so no test sees another's changes. `toBe` (`Object.is`) is right for a number; `toEqual` would also pass but signals "comparing structure", which a number doesn't have.

prompts.prompt: Assert that an async function rejects, in a form that means the same thing in every Vitest version.
prompts.explanation: `.rejects` unwraps the rejection and applies `toThrow` to it; the assertion is itself a promise, so `await` it. Vitest 4 would auto-await a dangling one with a warning, Vitest 5 fails it even when it's right, and Node's runner marks the test passed before the check runs — only the awaited form means the same thing everywhere.

prompts.prompt: Make `toThrow` able to catch the synchronous error.
prompts.explanation: Wrapping the call in a function delays it: `expect` calls it inside a `try` and checks what was thrown. Without the wrapper, the error escapes while the argument is being evaluated.
`0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, so `toBe(0.3)` fails. `toBeCloseTo` compares to a number of decimal places (2 by default).

prompts.prompt: Use Node's built-in assertions in strict mode, and compare two objects by structure.
prompts.explanation: `node:assert/strict` turns the legacy `==` comparisons into strict ones; there, `deepEqual` is the same as `deepStrictEqual`. `assert.equal` would compare the two arrays by identity and fail.

code: it("C", () => expect({ name: "Ada", nick: undefined }).toEqual({ name: "Ada" }));
snippets.question: Which of A, B and C pass?
snippets.answer: A and C pass; B fails
acceptable: A, C pass and B fails
snippets.explanation: `toEqual` compares own enumerable structure: it ignores the class (A) and treats an `undefined`-valued key as missing (C). `toStrictEqual` adds both checks, so a `User` instance isn't equal to a plain object (B). Reach for `toStrictEqual` when the class or an explicit `undefined` is part of the contract.

// The only test in the file. Run with `vitest run` (Vitest 4).
snippets.question: What does Vitest report for this test, and what is the exit code?
snippets.explanation: `forEach` calls each async callback and throws away the promise it returns, so the test function's own promise resolves immediately — before either 10 ms timer fires. The test is reported passed, the worker shuts down, and the failing `expect`s never run where anyone is listening. Use `for…of` with `await`, or `await Promise.all(...)`.

code: const fetchUser = async (id: number) => ({ id, name: "Ada" });
snippets.question: Under Vitest 4, does this test pass or fail?
snippets.answer: It fails, with a warning that the assertion wasn't awaited
snippets.explanation: Vitest 4 tracks un-awaited `.resolves`/`.rejects` assertions and awaits them when the test ends, so the wrong expectation still fails — alongside a warning that the next major will fail the test for the missing `await` (Vitest 5 does). The safety net is Vitest's, not JavaScript's: Node's runner marks the equivalent un-awaited `assert.rejects` test passed and only reports the failure afterwards, as activity after the test ended. Always write the `await`.
